chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
title: Ornette Coleman: weak alto but ingenious composer
summary: Mingus doubts his intonation but praises his sense of composition and says many copy him.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Do you see that changing at all in some of the newer people composing more that you've heard?

Yeah, there's a guy, he got -- I mean, when he first got out of New York in '59, sure, there was a lot of controversy and a lot of people put him down, but he got a lot of publicity and record contracts. Then, all of a sudden -- not all of a sudden, but after a few years, he had the damndest time making a living. Was it because his music was too advanced or what?
No, but he can't play alto.

See, I didn't know how bad he was. He may be better now. But I was in Los Angeles and this lady says, you think Artie can blow, don't you? (Inaudible) and he put on a record with a piano player. ________ was trying to play songs.
He was trying to play Charlie Parker.
It was the most ridiculous intonation I ever heard in my life. But, see, you take a piano ________, which gives you a set pitch.

And just put a bass, move it around, and a drum, you can get away with playing the ________ all night long, and that's about what he does. (Inaudible) he was playing jazz. I don't know what he's doing when he's playing rock and roll. But he has an ingenious sense of composition.
Yeah. He has very strong melodic lines, and when I hear some of the people after him, the so-called avant garde --
A lot of guys copy him now.
Yeah. I always hear ________ somewhere or another.
